Every one of those rows was earned. The deliveries, riders, offers and earnings in this database were created by running the product: the demo seed registers a real rider through the public API, a staff member approves each document, the rider goes online, a customer books, the rider accepts and delivers. No figure on any dashboard is typed in, and the seed refuses to invent revenue.

Phase 6 — the dispatch engine

A booking must find a rider without anyone watching the screen. Phase 4 proved that two riders cannot hold the same job. Phase 6 makes that race run itself: it offers in batches, widens when nobody answers, and finally tells a human instead of going quiet.

DecisionHow it works
The search widens in roundsRound 1 asks the three closest riders within 5 km; then 12 km, 25 km and finally the whole branch. Each round lasts one offer window, and a round that finds nobody still counts — that is what lets the next one reach further out.
The round is data, not memorydeliveries.dispatchRound survives restarts, deploys and any number of API processes. No worker holds the state of a live dispatch in a variable.
A no is permanentA rider who rejects a job is never asked about it again. Riders asked in the round that just ended sit out one round, then return to the pool — a rider who was driving is not a rider who refused.
Eligibility is a filter, not a scoreApproved documents, approved application, online, active account, and under the active-job limit. Capacity is enforced by the query, so a rider at their limit is never offered work.
Ranking is transparentDistance to the pickup, plus 25 km for a stale location ping, plus a small 3 km penalty for being outside the delivery's zone.
One round at a timeA per-delivery Redis lock (SET PX 15000 NX) means two API processes, or a double click, cannot double-offer. A concurrent test drives two ticks at once.
Giving up is loudWhen the schedule is spent the engine raises one DISPATCH_EXHAUSTED alert (guarded by a 10-minute Redis key) and stops. It will not restart by itself when a rider frees up — that job needs a decision.
The socket never owns the truthPushes say only something changed; the screen refetches through the REST API. Every action still needs a bearer token and a permission — the live channel is notification, not authority.

Phase 4 — the rider portal, offers and the delivery workflow

Two riders can never hold the same job. That is the whole point of this phase, and it is enforced in the database and in Redis rather than in the UI. An offer is a row with an expiry; accepting it takes a short Redis lock, claims the rider's own assignment with a conditional update, moves the delivery from PENDING to ACCEPTED in the same transaction, and only then expires the rival offers. A loser of the race gets a clean 409 DELIVERY_TAKEN — never a 500, never a double assignment.

RuleHow it works
Offer window20 seconds by default (DISPATCH_OFFER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS). The deadline is stored on the row; the countdown in the browser is display only.
Who gets offeredApproved riders in the delivery's branch who are ONLINE, under their concurrent-job limit, ranked by haversine distance from their latest ping (or their zone centre, pushed down the list, if the ping is stale). The best three are offered.
AcceptingRedis SET NX PX token lock → conditional updateMany on the rider's own assignment → conditional delivery claim PENDING → ACCEPTED → rival offers expired after commit.
Expiry and refusalAn expired offer is swept and can be re-offered later; an explicit refusal is respected and that rider is never offered the same job again. Both leave the delivery waiting for someone else.
Someone must be onlineA paid booking placed while every rider is offline is not stranded: going online triggers a sweep that offers waiting deliveries immediately.
CommissionPercentage from the pricing rule, frozen into deliveries.commissionSnapshot at acceptance. Changing the rate tomorrow cannot change what this rider is owed.
Proof of deliveryThe recipient's 6-digit code (SHA-256, 5 attempts) or a photo plus the recipient's name. Either way the delivery completes once and the earning is written once.
Going onlineRefused with a specific reason when the account is not approved, the account is suspended, or a required document is not approved — and it names the missing document.

Phase 4 — the admin side of onboarding

A rider cannot approve themselves. Staff review each document and then the application, and both decisions are written to the audit trail with before/after values. The Phase 5 admin screens will call exactly these endpoints.

RuleHow it works
Permissions, not one big admin passReading the queue needs rider:read, reviewing or approving needs rider:approve, and streaming a document's bytes needs rider:document:read — a support agent holds none of them.
Documents are privateStored under riders/<id>/documents/ with no public URL. The only read path is an authenticated, permission-checked endpoint that returns Cache-Control: private, no-store.
No approval without papersApproving a rider while any required document is unapproved returns 409 DOCUMENTS_INCOMPLETE naming them — the same rule the rider's own "go online" check uses.
Rejection needs a reasonThe rider reads it. A re-upload resets the document to PENDING so nobody is stuck forever.
Suspension takes effect immediatelyStatus becomes SUSPENDED, availability is forced OFFLINE, and the rider's next attempt to go online is refused.

Phase 3 — booking and the pricing engine

The browser never sends a price. A booking request carries two coordinates, a package description and a delivery type. The API looks up the active pricing rule, measures the route, assembles the fee, applies promotions and returns the breakdown. When the customer confirms, it calculates all of it again — a quote is never treated as a payment instruction.

StepRule
ZoneThe zone containing the pickup decides the rule; falls back to the branch rule, then the global rule. A point more than 60 km from every zone is refused with a readable message.
DistanceHaversine × 1.35 road factor while Google Maps is stubbed. Multi-stop trips are summed leg by leg.
FeesBase fee + (distance beyond the free kilometres × per-km rate) + additional stops.
MinimumThe floor is applied to the trip before surcharges, so it protects the trip without hiding an express fee.
SurchargesExpress, same-day and scheduled fees from the rule row.
RoundingOne rounding step, to 50 kobo, in integer arithmetic. No floating-point naira in the money path.
PromotionsPercentage (capped), fixed amount, or free delivery. Window, global limit, per-customer limit and minimum order are all checked against the database. A promo can make a delivery free, never negative.
FreezeThe entire breakdown is written to deliveries.priceSnapshot. A rule change tomorrow cannot alter what was charged today.

Phase 2 — authentication and access control

Three portals share one API, so the central question is who may do what. Phase 2 answers it in four layers, all enforced on the server. Hiding a button in React is a courtesy, never a control — every one of these rules is re-checked by the API on every request.

LayerHow it works
PasswordsArgon2id (memory-hard, winner of the Password Hashing Competition). Stored hashes begin $argon2id$. A leaked database does not hand out passwords.
Sessions15-minute access JWT kept in memory; long-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie that JavaScript cannot read. Every refresh rotates the token and revokes the previous one.
Reuse detectionIf an already-rotated refresh token is presented again, a copy has leaked: the entire session family is revoked and the event is logged.
AuthorisationA global guard denies everything by default; routes must opt in with @Public(). Staff routes then need an explicit permission such as withdrawal:approve. Portal type is checked separately, so a customer token can never act as staff.
Account protection5 failed logins lock the account for 15 minutes; Redis-backed rate limits on every sensitive route return 429 with a "wait N seconds" message.
EvidenceAn append-only audit table records every registration, login, failure, lockout, password change and permission change — with IP, user agent and before/after values, and never a password or token.

How to view the live app yourself

A localhost link cannot work from your computer — that address only exists inside the sandbox machine where the code runs. Use the preview panel in this conversation instead: any server I start (the web app on port 5173, the API on port 4000) appears there as a live, clickable preview.

If the preview is not visible, ask me to restart the servers — the sandbox resets between sessions, which stops the processes and wipes the installed packages, but never touches your code.

Rebuilding from a cold sandbox

# one command: services + install + migrate + seed
npm run setup

# then start both servers (preview appears automatically)
npm run dev

# verify
npm test            # 149 tests against a real, isolated Postgres + Redis
bash scripts/smoke.sh
node scripts/seed-demo-phase4.mjs     # a real rider, approved, online, with an offer
node scripts/capture-phase4.mjs       # rider journey + refresh these screenshots
node scripts/capture-phase3.mjs       # booking journey
python3 scripts/build-report.py       # regenerate this page

Known limitations after Phase 4

  • Email and SMS are console drivers. Codes print to the API log, and in development are also returned to the browser so the flow can be tested without spend. A real provider plugs into MessagingService in Phase 7 without touching the auth code.
  • No staff 2FA yet. Recommended before real money moves; the TOTP storage and verification plumbing already exist.
  • Google Maps is not connected. Distances are straight-line × a road factor, and the UI labels them as an estimate. A real key switches one service, nothing else.
  • No payment is taken yet. A booking is created UNPAID and the screen says so; Paystack, Flutterwave and the wallet arrive in Phase 7. Riders are already earning into a real ledger — the money is recorded, not yet collected or paid out.
  • Offers are polled, not pushed. The rider app checks every few seconds; Socket.IO push and BullMQ queues arrive in Phase 6. The 20-second deadline is enforced server-side either way.
  • The waiting-delivery sweep runs on a rider coming online, not on a timer. A delivery that finds no rider waits until someone goes online or an admin assigns it (Phase 5); the scheduled worker joins it in Phase 6.
  • Not yet built: admin document-review screens (the API is live and tested), staff/role management screens, audit-log viewer, session list, withdrawals. The screens arrive with Phases 5–7.
  • Payments remain simulated (PAYMENTS_MODE=DEVELOPMENT) until the live keys are placed in the server's .env — never in this workspace.
